L8: # Quantum Tensor Networks, Stochastic Processes, and Weighted Automata
L9: 
L10: Sandesh Adhikary, Siddarth Srinivasan, Jacob Miller, Guillaume Rabusseau, Byron Boots
L11: 
L12: Proceedings of The 24th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics, PMLR 130:2080-2088, 2021.
L13: #### Abstract
L14: Modeling joint probability distributions over sequences has been studied from many perspectives. The physics community developed matrix product states, a tensor-train decomposition for probabilistic modeling, motivated by the need to tractably model many-body systems. But similar models have also been studied in the stochastic processes and weighted automata literature, with little work on how these bodies of work relate to each other.
L15: We address this gap by showing how stationary or uniform versions of popular quantum tensor network models have equivalent representations in the stochastic processes and weighted automata literature, in the limit of infinitely long sequences.
L16: We demonstrate several equivalence results between models used in these three communities: (i) uniform variants of matrix product states, Born machines and locally purified states from the quantum tensor networks literature, (ii) predictive state representations, hidden Markov models, norm-observable operator models and hidden quantum Markov models from the stochastic process literature, and (iii) stochastic weighted automata, probabilistic automata and quadratic automata from the formal languages literature.
L17: Such connections may open the door for results and methods developed in one area to be applied in another.

L22@P0: Abstract
L23@P0: Modeling joint probability distributions over
L24@P0: sequences has been studied from many perspectives. The physics community developed matrix
L25@P0: product states, a tensor-train decomposition for
L26@P0: probabilistic modeling, motivated by the need
L27@P0: to tractably model many-body systems. But
L28@P0: similar models have also been studied in the
L29@P0: stochastic processes and weighted automata literature, with little work on how these bodies of
L30@P0: work relate to each other. We address this gap
L31@P0: by showing how stationary or uniform versions
L32@P0: of popular quantum tensor network models
L33@P0: have equivalent representations in the stochastic
L34@P0: processes and weighted automata literature,
L35@P0: in the limit of infinitely long sequences. We
L36@P0: demonstrate several equivalence results between
L37@P0: models used in these three communities: (i)
L38@P0: uniform variants of matrix product states,
L39@P0: Born machines and locally purified states from
L40@P0: the quantum tensor networks literature, (ii)
L41@P0: predictive state representations, hidden Markov
L42@P0: models, norm-observable operator models and
L43@P0: hidden quantum Markov models from the
L44@P0: stochastic process literature, and (iii) stochastic
L45@P0: weighted automata, probabilistic automata and
L46@P0: quadratic automata from the formal languages
L47@P0: literature. Such connections may open the door
L48@P0: for results and methods developed in one area
L49@P0: to be applied in another.
L50@P0: Proceedings of the 24th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics (AISTATS) 2021, San Diego, California,
L51@P0: USA. PMLR: Volume 130. Copyright 2021 by the author(s).
L52@P0: 1 Introduction
L53@P0: Matrix product states (MPS) were first developed by
L54@P0: the physics community as compact representations of
L55@P0: often intractable wave functions of complex quantum
L56@P0: systems (Perez-Garcia et al., 2006; Kl¨umper et al., 1993;
L57@P0: Fannes et al., 1992), in parallel with the equivalent
L58@P0: tensor-train decomposition (Oseledets, 2011) developed in
L59@P0: applied mathematics for high-order tensors. These tensor
L60@P0: network models have been gaining popularity in machine
L61@P0: learning, especially as means of compressing highlyparameterized models (Novikov et al., 2015; Garipov
L62@P0: et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2017; Novikov et al., 2014). There
L63@P0: has also been recent interest in directly connecting ideas
L64@P0: and methods from quantum tensor networks to machine
L65@P0: learning (Stoudenmire and Schwab, 2016; Han et al.,
L66@P0: 2018; Guo et al., 2018; Huggins et al., 2019). In particular,
L67@P0: tensor networks have been used for probabilistic modeling
L68@P0: as parameterizations of joint probability tensors (Glasser
L69@P0: et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2021; Stokes and Terilla, 2019).
L70@P0: But the same problem has also been studied from various
L71@P0: other perspectives. Notably, observable operator models
L72@P0: (Jaeger, 2000) or predictive state representations (PSRs)
L73@P0: (Singh et al., 2004) from the machine learning literature
L74@P0: and stochastic weighted automata (Balle et al., 2014b) are
L75@P0: approaches to tackle essentially the same problem. While
L76@P0: Thon and Jaeger (2015) provide an overview discussing
L77@P0: connections between PSRs and stochastic weighted automata, their connection to MPS has not been extensively
L78@P0: explored. At the same time, there exist many variants of
L79@P0: tensor network models related to MPS that can be used
L80@P0: for probabilistic modeling. Glasser et al. (2019) recently
L81@P0: provided a thorough investigation of the relative expressiveness of various tensor networks for the non-uniform
L82@P0-1: * denotes equal contributionQuantum Tensor Networks, Stochastic Processes, and Weighted Automata
L83@P1: case (where cores in the tensor decomposition need not
L84@P1: be identical). However, to the best of our knowledge,
L85@P1: similar relationships have not yet been established for the
L86@P1: uniform case. We address these issues by examining how
L87@P1: various quantum tensor networks relate to aforementioned
L88@P1: work in different fields, and we derive a collection of
L89@P1: results analyzing the relationships in expressiveness
L90@P1: between uniform MPS and their various subclasses.
L91@P1: The uniform case is important to examine for a number
L92@P1: of reasons. The inherent weight sharing in uniform tensor
L93@P1: networks leads to particularly compact models, especially
L94@P1: when learning from highly structured data. This compactness becomes especially useful when we consider physical
L95@P1: implementations of tensor network models in quantum
L96@P1: circuits. For instance, Glasser et al. (2019) draw an equivalence between local quantum circuits and tensor networks;
L97@P1: network parameters define gates that can be implemented
L98@P1: on a quantum computer for probabilistic modeling.
L99@P1: Uniform networks have fewer parameters, corresponding
L100@P1: to a smaller set of quantum gates and greater ease of implementation on resource constrained near-term quantum
L101@P1: computers. Despite the many useful properties of uniformity, the tensor-network literature tends to focus more on
L102@P1: non-uniform models. We aim to fill this gap by developing
L103@P1: expressiveness relationships for uniform variants.
L104@P1: We expect that the connections established in this paper
L105@P1: will also open the door for results and methods in one area
L106@P1: to be applied in another. For instance, one of the proof
L107@P1: strategies we adopt is to develop expressiveness relationships between subclasses of PSRs, and show how they also
L108@P1: carry over to equivalent uniform tensor networks. Such
L109@P1: cross fertilization also takes place at the level of algorithms.
L110@P1: For instance, the learning algorithm for locally purified
L111@P1: states (LPS) employed in Glasser et al. (2019) does not
L112@P1: preserve uniformity of the model across time-steps, or
L113@P1: enforce normalization constraints on learned operators.
L114@P1: With the equivalence between uniform LPS and hidden
L115@P1: quantum Markov models (HQMMs) established in this
L116@P1: paper, the HQMM learning algorithm from Adhikary et al.
L117@P1: (2020), based on optimization over the Stiefel manifold,
L118@P1: can be adapted to learn uniform LPS while enforcing
L119@P1: all appropriate constraints. Similarly, spectral algorithms
L120@P1: that have been developed for stochastic process models
L121@P1: such as hidden Markov models (HMMs) and PSRs (Hsu
L122@P1: et al., 2012; Siddiqi et al., 2010; Bailly et al., 2009) could
L123@P1: also be adapted to learn uniform LPS and uniform MPS
L124@P1: models. Spectral algorithms typically come with consistency guarantees, along with rigorous bounds on sample
L125@P1: complexity. Such formal guarantees are less common in
L126@P1: tensor network methods, such as variants of alternating
L127@P1: least squares (Oseledets, 2011) or density matrix renormalization group methods (White, 1992). On the other hand,
L128@P1: tensor network algorithms tend to be better suited for very
L129@P1: high-dimensional data; presenting an opportunity to adapt
L130@P1: them to scale up algorithms for stochastic process models.
L131@P1: Finally, one of our key motivations is to simply provide
L132@P1: a means of translating between similar models developed
L133@P1: in different fields. While prior works (Glasser et al., 2019;
L134@P1: Kliesch et al., 2014; Critch and Morton, 2014) have noted
L135@P1: similarities between tensor networks, stochastic processes
L136@P1: and weighted automata, many formal and explicit
L137@P1: connections are still lacking, especially in the context of
L138@P1: model expressiveness. It is still difficult for practitioners
L139@P1: in one field to verify that the model classes they have
L140@P1: been working with are indeed used elsewhere, given the
L141@P1: differences in nomenclature and domain of application;
L142@P1: simply having a thesaurus to rigorously translate between
L143@P1: fields can be quite valuable. Such a thesaurus is
L144@P1: particularly timely given the growing popularity of tensor
L145@P1: networks in machine learning. We hope that the connections developed in this paper will help bring together
L146@P1: complementary advances occurring in these various fields.
L147@P1: Summary of Contributions In Section 2, we demonstrate that uniform Matrix product states (uMPS) are
L148@P1: equivalent to predictive state representations and stochastic weighted automata, when taken in the non-terminating
L149@P1: limit (where we evaluate probabilities sufficiently away
L150@P1: from the end of a sequence). Section 3 presents the known
L151@P1: equivalence between uMPS with non-negative parameters,
L152@P1: HMMs, and probabilistic automata, to show in Section
L153@P1: 4 that another subclass of uMPS called Born machines
L154@P1: (BM) (Han et al., 2018) is equivalent to norm-observable
L155@P1: operator models (NOOM) (Zhao and Jaeger, 2010) and
L156@P1: quadratic weighted automata (QWA) (Bailly, 2011). We
L157@P1: also demonstrate that uBMs and NOOMs are relatively
L158@P1: restrictive model classes in that there are HMMs with
L159@P1: no equivalent finite-dimensional uBM or NOOM (HMMs
L160@P1: * NOOMs/uBMs). Finally, in Section 5, we analyze a
L161@P1: broadly expressive subclass of uMPS known as locally purified states (LPS), demonstrate its equivalence to hidden
L162@P1: quantum Markov models (HQMMs), and discuss the open
L163@P1: question of how the expressiveness of uLPS relates to that
L164@P1: of uMPS. We thus develop a unifying perspective on a
L165@P1: wide range of models coming from different communities,
L166@P1: providing a rigorous characterization of how they are
L167@P1: related to one another, as illustrated in Figures 1 and 2.
L168@P1: The proofs for all theorems are provided in the Appendix.
L169@P1: In our presentation, we routinely point out connections
L170@P1: between tensor networks and relevant concepts in physics.
L171@P1: However, we note that these models are not restricted
L172@P1: to this domain. Furthermore, we focus on models with
L173@P1: a finite number of outcomes or observations, also called
L174@P1: alphabets in the formal language community. This is the
L175@P1: most commonly used setting for the models we consider,
L176@P1: and does not really restrict the applicability of our results.
L177@P1: Notation We use bold-face for matrix and tensor
L178@P1-2: operators (e.g. A), arrows over symbols to denote vectorsSandesh Adhikary∗
L179@P2: , Siddarth Srinivasan∗, Jacob Miller, Guillaume Rabusseau, Byron Boots

L182@P2: (column-first convention) of matrices. We frequently
L183@P2: make use of the ones matrix 1 (filled with 1s) and the
L184@P2: identity matrix I, as well as their vectorizations ~1 and ~I.
L185@P2: We use overhead bars to denote complex conjugates (e.g.
L186@P2: A¯ ) and † for the conjugate transpose (A¯ T =A†). Finally,
L187@P2: tr(·) denotes the trace operation applied to matrices, and

L189@P2: 2 Uniform Matrix Product States
L190@P2: Given a sequence of N observations, where each outcome
L191@P2: can take di values, the joint probability of any particular
L192@P2: sequence y1,...,yN can be written using the following
L193@P2: tensor-train decomposition, which gives an MPS:
L194@P2: P(y1,...,yN) ∝ MPSy1,...,yN
L195@P2: =A[N],yN A[N−1],yN−1... A[2],y2A[1],y1(1)
L196@P2: where each A[i]is a three-mode tensor core of the MPS
L197@P2: containing di slices, with the matrix slice associated with
L198@P2: outcome Yi denoted by A[i],yi. The above joint probability
L199@P2: distribution must be normalized through a partition function. A common strategy to efficiently compute this partition function is to convert the tensor chain into a canonical
L200@P2: form wherein expensive tensor contractions reduce to
L201@P2: the identity. Each matrix slice A[i],yiis a Di+1 × Di
L202@P2: matrix, and the conventional choice (which we use in this
L203@P2: paper) of open boundary conditions is to set D0=DN =1
L204@P2: (i.e. A[1],y1 and A[N],yN are column and row vectors
L205@P2: respectively). MPS with open boundaries are equivalent
L206@P2: to tensor train (TT) decompositions, and we will define
L207@P2: them over the complex field, a choice common in quantum
L208@P2: physics and tensor network settings. The maximal value
L209@P2: of D=maxkDk is also called the bond-dimension or the
L210@P2: TT-rank (Glasser et al., 2019) of the MPS. For fixed
L211@P2: dynamics, this will lead the MPS cores A[i]to be identical.
L212@P2: In this paper, we will focus on the “uniform” case of
L213@P2: identical cores, i.e., a uniform MPS or uMPS. uMPS
L214@P2: models were first developed in the quantum physics
L215@P2: community (Perez-Garcia et al., 2006; Vanderstraeten
L216@P2: et al., 2019), although employing a different probabilistic
L217@P2: correspondence (Born machines as discussed later) than
L218@P2: described below. As we will discuss, this corresponds naturally to Markovian dynamical systems; the notion of past
L219@P2: An alternate choice, periodic boundary conditions, sets
L220@P2: D0=DN ≥1 and uses a trace operation to evaluate the product of matrices in Equation 1. MPS with periodic boundaries
L221@P2: are equivalent to the tensor ring decomposition (Mickelin and
L222@P2: Karaman, 2018).
L223@P2: Operational characterizations of the bond dimension have
L224@P2: been developed in quantum physics, in terms of entanglement (Eisert et al., 2010) or the state space dimension of
L225@P2: recurrent many-body dynamics which generate the associated
L226@P2: wavefunction (Schoen et al., 2005).

L236@P2: by the tensor train structure where each core only has

L245@P2: To explore connections with arbitrary-length PSRs and
L246@P2: WFAs, we will particularly focus on the non-terminating
L247@P2: limit. Consider that if we wished to compute the

L258@P2: Definition 1 (Non-terminating uMPS). A nonterminating uMPS is an infinitely long uMPS where
L259@P2: we can compute the probability of any sequence
L260@P2: P(y1, ... , yT ) of length T by marginalizing over infinitely many future observations, i.e. P(y1,...,yT ) =

L265@P2-3: P(y1,...,yT ,yT+1,...,yN).Quantum Tensor Networks, Stochastic Processes, and Weighted Automata
L266@P3: This is a natural approach to modeling arbitrary length sequences with Markovian dynamics; intuitively, if given an
L267@P3: identical set of tensor cores at each time step, the probability of a sequence should not depend on how far it is from
L268@P3: the ‘end’ of the sequence. Similar notions are routinely
L269@P3: used in machine learning and physics. In machine learning,
L270@P3: it is common to discard the first few entries of sequences
L271@P3: as “burn-in” to allow systems to reach their stationary
L272@P3: distribution. In our case, the burn is being applied to the
L273@P3: end of the sequence. The non-terminating limit is also
L274@P3: similar to the “thermodynamic limit” employed in manybody physics, which marginalizes over an infinite number
L275@P3: of future and past observations (Vanderstraeten et al.,
L276@P3: 2019). Such limits reflect the behavior seen in the interior
L277@P3: of large systems, and avoid more complicated phenomena
L278@P3: which arise near the beginning or end of sequences.
L279@P3: 2.1 The Many Names of Matrix Product States
L280@P3: While connections between MPS and hidden Markov
L281@P3: models (HMM) have been widely noted, we point out
L282@P3: that non-terminating uMPS models have been studied
L283@P3: from various perspectives, and are referred to by different names in the literature, such as stochastic weighted
L284@P3: finite automata (stochastic WFA) (Balle et al., 2014a),
L285@P3: quasi-realizations (Vidyasagar, 2011), observable operator
L286@P3: models (OOM) (Jaeger, 2000), and (uncontrolled) predictive state representations (PSR) (Singh et al., 2004). The
L287@P3: latter three models are exactly identical (we just refer to
L288@P3: them as uncontrolled PSRs in this paper) and come from
L289@P3: the stochastic processes perspective, while stochastic WFA
L290@P3: are slightly different in their formulation, in that they are
L291@P3: more similar to (terminating) uMPS (see below). Thon
L292@P3: and Jaeger (2015) detail a general framework of sequential
L293@P3: systems to study how PSRs and WFA relate to each other.
L294@P3: Predictive State Representations We write the
L295@P3: stochastic process defined by an n–dimensional predictive
L296@P3: state representation over a set of discrete observations O as
L297@P3: a tuple (C
L298@P3: n, ~σ, {τ y}y∈O, ~x0). The initial state ~x0∈Cn is
